title: Wireless epidural BCI lets a man quadriplegic for 14 years drink unaided (NEO, Xuanwu Hospital and Tsinghua)
summary: 54-year-old man, quadriplegic for 14 years, drank unaided by driving a pneumatic glove through the NEO epidural BCI; announced 29 Jan 2024.
account: On 24 October 2023, teams led by Zhao Guoguang at Xuanwu Hospital and Hong Bo at Tsinghua University implanted the NEO wireless epidural brain-computer interface in a 54-year-old man with complete C4 spinal cord injury (ASIA A) from a car accident, quadriplegic for 14 years. Discharged ten days later, he trained at home for three months. At a trial-phase summary meeting on 29 January 2024 the joint team announced that he could drive a pneumatic glove with his brain activity to drink water unaided, with grasp-decoding accuracy above 90% and improved ASIA scores and somatosensory evoked potentials. A September 2024 preprint reported nine months of home use: a 0.91 grasp-detection F1-score, eating and drinking, and a 27-point ARAT gain.
purpose: NEO was built to let people with tetraplegia control external equipment, including a pneumatic exoskeleton glove, from epidural brain signals, for assistance and hand-function rehabilitation at home; restoring this patient's grasp so that he could drink was exactly that purpose.
system: NEO (Neural Electronic Opportunity) wireless minimally invasive epidural brain-computer interface: eight epidural electrodes over the sensorimotor cortex, a battery-free coin-sized skull implant powered and read through the scalp, and a Riemannian-geometry grasp-intention decoder driving a pneumatic exoskeleton glove
developer: Tsinghua University School of Medicine, Prof. Hong Bo's team, with Neuracle Medical Technology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (博睿康科技), the trial sponsor
deployer: Xuanwu Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing (teams of Zhao Guoguang and Shan Yongzhi)
segment: Neurotechnology and spinal cord injury rehabilitation
taxonomy_note: The benefit is restored hand function and independence for a person with tetraplegia; the taxonomy has no 'restored physical function' class, so it is filed under accessibility, and the measured neurological recovery (ARAT +27) is a health outcome the taxonomy does not name.

ratings.reason: After 14 years of complete quadriplegia the patient regained the ability to drink and eat by himself through the BCI-driven glove, and the preprint reports neurological recovery: upper-limb motor score +5, ARAT +27, and the ability to hold objects without the BCI.

ai_role.statement: The AI contribution is the decoder: a Riemannian-geometry classifier, calibrated in about ten minutes on beta, low-gamma and high-gamma features of eight-channel epidural ECoG, with a hidden Markov model for temporal smoothing, that detects grasp intention and triggers the pneumatic glove. The preprint reports 94% calibration accuracy, a grasp-detection F1-score rising above 0.9 after three months (average 0.91 over nine months), and 100% object-transfer success with the BCI against 35% without it. The electrodes, implant, surgery and glove are not AI; the authors attribute the later neurological recovery to repeated BCI training, not to the decoder alone.

produced_by: Eight chronic epidural electrodes over the sensorimotor cortex of a patient whose cortex still generated grasp-related signals after 14 years of complete C4 injury
A grasp-intention decoder calibrated in about ten minutes and robust to the signal drift and chewing artefacts of home use
A battery-free implant powered and read through the scalp, so the patient could train at home daily after discharge ten days post-surgery
A wearable pneumatic glove able to execute the decoded grasp on the patient's right hand, which retained limited forearm movement
must_hold: The patient's motor cortex must still produce decodable grasp intention despite years of paralysis
The decoder must stay accurate without frequent recalibration across months of home use
The patient or a caregiver must be able to attach the external coil and the glove for daily sessions
Neurological recovery beyond assisted grasping is a single-patient finding and must be reproduced in further patients
